title: Prevalence of meditation-related adverse effects in a population-based sample in the United States

selection.evidence: NOTES: 'schlosser2019 gave a flat lifetime prevalence ... This is a population sample' (testing my finding's generality).

cost.compute_notes: Author-hosted PDF (15 pp). No individual data located: the paper cites two OSF preregistrations; the OSF API did not answer within 60 s on 2026-10-16 ~15:30 (it served other requests at 14:52), so availability is unchecked, not negative. Per-bin rates are not in the main text; recovered from Figure 1's vector paths with PyMuPDF (reanalysis/g1_figure_extract.py) and checked three independent ways. Dose-response fits and 400 known-answer simulations: about a minute.

claims.statement: Among US adults with lifetime meditation exposure (n = 434 of 953 screened, Prolific representative sampling), 32.3% endorsed any meditation-related adverse effect on a single item, 50.0% at least one MRAES-MBP item, 10.4% effects lasting >= 1 month, and 10.6% some functional impairment (1.2% lasting >= 1 month).
claims.scope: Online panel, quota-matched on age, gender and race; lifetime-ever items; self-attributed causation.

quantities.name: prevalence_any_mrae_single_item
quantities.source: Table I; Figure 1 Total bar reproduces it (calibration bar)

our_assessment.why: Internally consistent: the figure, the table and the text agree, and every per-bin percentage times its bin size is an integer. Read beside schlosser2019 (25.6% single item, regular meditators, Europe/US): a population sample with modest practice reports MORE, not less. That is one more sign that a lifetime-ever item is not a cumulative-exposure measure.

claims.statement: Factors that may increase risk include practice-related variables (amount of meditation): greater lifetime hours was associated with MRAE (single item r = .10; MRAES-MBP total r = .14; impairment > 1 day r = .10).
claims.scope: Correlations with lifetime hours coded 1 = 0-10, 2 = 11-100, 3 = 101+ (Table I note), i.e. everyone from 101 to over 5,000 hours (n = 173) at one level.

quantities.name: delta_aic_cumulative_hazard_vs_best
quantities.baseline: constant per-hour hazard predicts .001 -> .98 across bins; best models are a saturating susceptible fraction (pi = .35 reached by 11-100 h) and an inverted U; quadratic vs linear in log hours LR chi2 8.56, p = .003 (impairment: p = .026; 1+ MRAES: p = .27, undecided)

quantities.name: known_answer_recovery_rate
quantities.unit: share of 200 simulated datasets in which AIC picks the generating model (susceptible-fraction generator; cumulative-hazard generator: 0.895)
quantities.baseline: same bin sizes as the paper

our_assessment.why: The association exists, but it is a step at the START of practice, not a dose-response. Prevalence nearly doubles from 0-10 h to 11-100 h and then stops rising; single-item MRAE and impairment are, if anything, LOWER above 1,000 h (inverted U, p = .003 and .026). A constant per-hour hazard is rejected by over 200 AIC units for every outcome. The three-level coding with a 101+ ceiling cannot show any of this, and 'amount of meditation' as a risk factor reads as a gradient that the data do not have. This is the second independent sample showing the shape found in schlosser2019 (flat lifetime prevalence by years of practice). It favours early-onset susceptibility, OR selective continuation by people who did not have adverse effects -- which c4 partly speaks to. High-hour bins are small (31-39), so the decline is suggestive, not established.

claims.statement: Figure 1 (and Supplemental Table 6) give the frequency of each MRAE outcome by lifetime meditation hours.

quantities.name: impairment_gt_1day_minus_any_impairment_5001plus
quantities.baseline: 'impairment > 1 day' is a subset of 'any impairment' by construction, so this must be <= 0; it is <= 0 in the other six groups

our_assessment.why: One group of bars is logically impossible: among the 32 participants with 5,001+ hours, 4 report impairment lasting more than a day but only 2 report any impairment. Either a bar is mis-drawn, the two outcomes are swapped in that group, or the underlying coding differs for that bin. It does not move any headline (totals agree with Table I), but it is a defect in the only place the per-bin data are published. Supplemental Table 6 would settle it; not retrieved.

claims.statement: Any meditation practice in the past 30 days was associated with greater likelihood of MRAE (single item r = .12; MRAES-MBP total r = .15); participants reporting MRAE were equally glad to have practised (87.9-88.2% vs 88.7% overall).
claims.scope: 34.8% of the sample had not meditated in the past 30 days.

quantities.name: r_current_practice_mrae_single_item
quantities.baseline: did not survive FDR for the single item; r = .15 for MRAES total

our_assessment.why: Not reanalysed (no individual data). It bears on an open question of schlosser2019: whether adverse effects make people stop, which a survey of current meditators cannot see. If MRAE drove discontinuation, lapsed practitioners would report MORE MRAE; here they report LESS. That argues against selective attrition as the explanation of the flat curve in c2, unless recall fades after stopping (salience). A weak, cross-sectional signal, but the first one on that question in this corpus.

artifacts.locator: Figure 1 vector paths in the author-hosted PDF https://jimhopper.com/pdf/goldberg_britton_et_al_2021.pdf (sha256 ec19d133...4af2749e); recovered values in reanalysis/figure1_bars.json

checked.result: 35 bars recovered. Calibrated on ONE bar (Total, single item = 32.26%). The other four Total bars reproduce Table I (50.0, 10.6, 6.0, 1.2); the 0-10 h group reproduces values back-calculated from the text's >= 11 h subgroup (19.5, 37.8, 6.1, 0.0); every percentage times its bin n is an integer, confirming the assumed group order.

relations.why: Mindfulness programmes narrow the outcome distribution on average (-6% SD), which invites 'nobody is made worse'. Goldberg's population sample has 10.6% reporting some functional impairment from meditation (1.2% lasting >= 1 month), and its risk appears in the first tens of hours -- inside a programme's dose. Both can be true: harms concentrated in a minority and in experiences (anxiety, traumatic re-experiencing) that RCT outcome scales may not register. A VR < 1 bounds harm on the measured scale only.

Independent population sample with the same structural result: lifetime prevalence of meditation-related adverse effects does not accumulate with practice; it appears early and plateaus (here, possibly declines). Also partly answers schlosser2019's open question about discontinuation (c4).
